synopsis: This survey organizes robotic world models by how prediction connects to action: as part of a policy, as a learned simulator, or as a generator of useful visual futures. Its central reading lesson is to track both the predictive representation and when it is used. Joint training, online imagination and real action execution are different claims. The benchmark compilation illustrates competitive methods across several architectures without establishing a universally superior design.

problem.text: The authors argue that reactive vision-language-action policies can struggle with long horizons and compounding errors because action prediction alone supplies insufficient foresight. They organize a fragmented literature around control-relevant prediction. Their definition includes both motor commands and semantic task instructions, while emphasizing that an actionable predictor must preserve consequences useful to robot decision making.

contributions.text: A policy-centered taxonomy separates decoupled inverse dynamics, shared video–action backbones, interacting experts, unified VLAs and latent predictive policies, while tracking inference-time future generation.

Two complementary views distinguish learned simulators for reinforcement learning/evaluation from video-model capabilities for imagination, controllability, structural consistency and reusable prediction.
A layered evaluation framework and dataset comparison connect predictive quality to control utility, with compiled manipulation results and explicit discussion of protocol fragmentation.

inputs: Surveyed systems: current observations, optionally proprioception and task/language instructions; controllable predictors also receive candidate motor actions.
outputs: Depending on role: future visual/latent/structured states, action chunks, imagined transitions, or policy/candidate assessment signals.

steps.name: Choose the predictive query
steps.detail: Section 3.1 treats future observations and actions as an idealized joint distribution. Marginalizing futures yields a policy; marginalizing actions yields passive prediction. Action-conditioned prediction asks what a proposed action causes, while inverse dynamics asks which actions explain a state transition. This conceptual relationship does not prove that implementations share one network.

steps.name: Locate the prediction–action interface
steps.detail: In the decoupled family, a world model supplies future frames or compact visual plans to a separate policy. Shared-backbone methods instead jointly process visual and action representations. MoT designs preserve specialized streams coupled through attention. The relevant distinction is parameterization and information flow, not merely whether losses are jointly optimized.

steps.name: Identify internal predictive supervision
steps.detail: Unified VLAs add future images or structured predictive outputs to action learning. Latent variants replace image reconstruction with future embeddings or conditions. FLARE aligns action-network features with future embeddings; VLA-JEPA uses future frames as target supervision. Symbolic transition models provide a complementary interface to high-level planning.

steps.name: Separate simulation from action selection
steps.detail: A learned simulator predicts transitions and possibly rewards or termination for imagined policy optimization. An evaluator instead scores proposed behaviors or policy checkpoints. Co-evolving systems refine the simulator using policy failures or real data before generating further training experience. Reliability of the imagined consequences matters in either role.

steps.name: Track video-model capability
steps.detail: The video-generation taxonomy progresses from imagined supervision to explicit action conditioning, then interaction/geometry priors and reusable foundation backbones. These are overlapping capabilities. IRASim's frame-level action conditioning illustrates control alignment; multi-view and geometric structure address consistency. Neither a plausible video nor an architectural label establishes executability.

steps.name: Transfer the questions across domains
steps.detail: Navigation uses predictions of unseen views to support planning under partial observability. Driving adds multi-agent evolution and structured scene representations such as occupancy or latent states. These applications broaden the organizing framework without making manipulation benchmark scores evidence for navigation or driving success.

training.text: There is no single survey training recipe. Decoupled predictors are typically pretrained and frozen or lightly adapted. Shared generators learn visual/action targets through diffusion, flow or discrete denoising objectives. Unified and latent policies can instead obtain predictive benefits through auxiliary supervision. The survey does not establish matched-data superiority of video pretraining over VLM pretraining.

Tables 3–4 compare action supervision, embodiment coverage, richer observations, language and contact signals, then their relevance to different modeling capabilities. These are qualitative, overlapping axes rather than measured dataset rankings. Section 7.2 highlights scarce failure-recovery and physically grounded supervision; it supplies no common data mixture or optimization budget.

inference.text: The visual branch may be fully generated, partially used, or omitted. The survey describes Cosmos Policy's direct mode as requiring actions, with future states and values used for planning; Fast-WAM uses video co-training while skipping test-time video. Therefore, training with a world-model objective does not by itself imply online rollout.

For simulator-based selection, the policy proposes actions and the world model predicts their consequences before ranking or replanning. Executed actions must still interact with the actual environment. A model's imagined reward or success estimate is a prediction whose fidelity requires separate evaluation.

equations.explanation: Equation (1): x_t is the modeled state, a is the low-level action sequence over horizon H, and l is the high-level task specification. The state representation is intentionally unrestricted. Language intent and motor intervention remain separate conditioning variables.

Equation (4): o denotes observations, a actions, l the instruction and k the chunk horizon. Equations (5)–(8) organize policy, passive prediction, controllable prediction and inverse dynamics as related queries. Reader analysis: the printed controllable and inverse-dynamics forms omit l; the survey does not establish the conditional independence needed to treat every displayed form as an exact conditional of Eq. (4).

results.setting: Spatial/Object/Goal/Long protocol; numbers compiled from cited methods, with no common training-budget or seed specification.
results.metric: Reported success rate (%) and directly reported four-suite average
results.interpretation: The equal rounded averages conceal different suite profiles, and high values occur across several coupling styles. These are compiled results, not a matched architecture ablation. No uncertainty is supplied; unreported entries remain missing.

results.task: RoboTwin simple and randomized manipulation (survey compilation)
results.setting: Table 6 RT-A: non-randomized testing; RT-B: harder randomized environments. Section 7.3 discusses RoboTwin 2.0.
results.interpretation: The profiles vary strongly with setting. The survey does not supply matched training conditions or uncertainty, so the differences cannot isolate world-model architecture or prove transfer to physical robots.

limitations.text: The source is a narrative survey with representative comparisons, not a new controlled experiment. Tables 5–6 cannot isolate the causal benefit of world modeling from pretraining, model size, data or deployment differences.

Protocol reporting is incomplete: Table 6 prints CALVIN labels as 'ABCD' and 'ABCDD' without clarifying train/test arrows, and slash-separated values are only identified as original protocol variants. Missing entries are not zero; the compilation contains no common uncertainty estimates.

The authors identify action-conditioning gaps, expensive iterative denoising, sparse nonvisual physical feedback, asynchronous sensor fusion, control guarantees and grounded symbolic abstraction as unresolved issues. These are research challenges rather than quantified failure rates for one model.

Predictive realism, policy-ranking fidelity and executability are different evaluation targets. Good appearance cannot establish reliable planning, and latent predictors need not render realistic videos to be useful.

reproduction.text: A faithful reconstruction of the survey's comparisons needs exact underlying paper versions, benchmark splits, embodiment/action conventions, training data, seeds and evaluation budgets. Tables 5–6 give useful row/column anchors but omit enough configuration that they are insufficient as standalone reproduction recipes.

Reader-proposed priorities are a controlled action-intervention test with fixed observations/instructions and a benchmark extraction audit preserving missing entries and protocol variants. These test the survey's causal-conditioning and comparison arguments; neither check was performed as an experiment here.

reasoning.text: The catalog correctly treats this as foundational survey/technical-resource work. The paper organizes multiple architectures and predictive mechanisms rather than proposing one deployable architecture. Its own five-family taxonomy supports leaving architecture, prediction paradigm and quadrant not applicable. Joint predictive-control notation or co-training does not justify assigning the survey itself to a One Model quadrant.

discussionQuestions: When does predictive co-training improve control without an inference-time world model?
Which action-sensitive diagnostic best predicts whether imagined policy rankings survive real execution?
What comparison controls are needed before attributing benchmark gains to a coupling architecture?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: The observed title and ordered 18-author list match the catalog. The PDF identifies arXiv:2605.00080v1, 30 April 2026, and lists nine institutions.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–4, Section 1; Figures 1–2 and contribution list
evidence.detail: The work surveys policy architectures, simulator applications and video-model capabilities. The timeline describes overlapping directions, not successive replacements.
World modeling predicts future states under physical actions and/or high-level instructions; state may be visual, latent, structured or symbolic. Visual plausibility alone is insufficient.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 2.2, Eq. (3); Section 3.1, Eqs. (4)–(8)
evidence.detail: The survey relates policy, passive prediction, controllable prediction and inverse dynamics through an idealized joint future-observation/action distribution. Here k is the action-chunk length.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 1, all paradigm groups and inference column
evidence.detail: Five policy families are compared by backbone, coupling and inference-time future generation. Fast-WAM skips test-time video; joint co-training and shared-backbone coupling are distinct labels.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 3.2, Eqs. (9)–(12); Figure 3(a) and caption
evidence.detail: A separate predictor supplies future observations or representations to an action policy. The predictor is typically pretrained, then frozen or lightly adapted; plausible but uncontrollable futures can propagate error.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 3.3, Figure 3(b), Eqs. (13)–(14)
evidence.detail: Shared backbones jointly model visual and action representations. Targets can be noise, velocity or masked tokens. Cosmos Policy separates direct action use from state/value-based planning; visual branches need not always run online.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10 and 12–13, Figure 3(c); Section 3.4, Eq. (15)
evidence.detail: Expert architectures retain modality-specific parameterization with repeated attention-based interaction. Fast-WAM is discussed as emphasizing video co-training over explicit test-time imagination.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 13–14, Figure 4 and caption; Section 3.5
evidence.detail: Unified VLAs combine actions with future-oriented supervision; WorldVLA uses future-image prediction mainly during training. Some unified systems retain specialized experts.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 14–15, Section 3.6
evidence.detail: FLARE aligns action-network features with future embeddings; VLA-JEPA uses future frames only as supervision targets. Latent prediction avoids image decoding; symbolic transitions are a complementary planner interface.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15–16, Section 4 introduction; Figure 5 and caption; Section 4.1, Eqs. (16)–(18)
evidence.detail: Learned simulators produce imagined transitions and optional reward/termination signals for policy optimization. Figure 5 contrasts policy updates with candidate scoring; its scores are schematic.

evidence.location: PDF p. 17, Section 4.1, Eq. (19) and surrounding discussion
evidence.detail: Policy failures or real interaction can refine a world model, whose improved imagined data then support policy updates; simulator reliability is part of the learning loop.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 17–18, Section 4.2
evidence.detail: World models rank or revise candidate actions, support planning, and compare policies/checkpoints. Hallucinations and long-horizon errors can corrupt evaluator signals.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 19–20, Figure 6 and caption; Sections 5.1–5.2 and Table 2
evidence.detail: Video-model capabilities span imagination-based supervision, action conditioning, structure-aware prediction and foundation-model reuse. The figure is an organizing schematic, not an experimentally validated pipeline.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 21–23, Sections 5.3–5.6
evidence.detail: Action alignment and interaction structure are emphasized. IRASim conditions individual frames on actions; structure includes masks, geometry and multi-view cues. Foundation backbones are adapted for interactive rollout and data generation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 23–24, Sections 6.1–6.2
evidence.detail: Navigation uses predicted unseen views and planning states; driving adds multi-agent dynamics, geometry, occupancy/latent representations and predictive supervision.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 24–26, Sections 7.1.1–7.1.3
evidence.detail: Evaluation separates open-loop prediction, closed-loop control/policy ranking, and physical or executability diagnostics. WorldEval checks policy ordering; WorldSimBench includes inverse-dynamics recovery.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 26–28, Tables 3–4 and Section 7.2
evidence.detail: Datasets are compared on overlapping supervision and capability axes. Checkmarks, dashes and crosses are qualitative grades; failure recovery and dense physical supervision are described as scarce.

evidence.location: PDF p. 28, Table 5, Cosmos Policy, LingBot-VA, Say-Dream-ACT, Motus and VLA-JEPA rows; header and footnotes
evidence.detail: Compiled LIBERO averages are respectively 98.5, 98.5, 98.1, 97.7 and 97.2. Cosmos Policy has 98.1/100.0/98.2/97.6 across Spatial/Object/Goal/Long; LingBot-VA has 98.5/99.6/97.2/98.5. Dashes denote unreported standard-protocol results.

evidence.location: PDF p. 29, Table 6, LingBot-VA, Motus and BagelVLA rows; all column footnotes; Section 7.3
evidence.detail: RoboTwin RT-A/RT-B values are 92.9/91.6, 88.7/87.0 and 75.3/20.9 respectively. RT-A is non-randomized and RT-B randomized. CALVIN labels print ABCD/ABCDD; paired SIMPLER entries denote unspecified original protocol variants. Strict ranking is cautioned against.

evidence.location: PDF p. 30, Sections 8.1–8.2
evidence.detail: Weak conditioning may follow intent rather than pending actions. Video denoising creates latency; partial denoising, latent modeling and training-only prediction are discussed as efficiency routes.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 30–31, Sections 8.3–8.5
evidence.detail: Open issues include force/tactile sensing, asynchronous modality alignment, MPC cost, formal control guarantees and grounded symbolic abstractions.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 28–31, Section 7.3 and Tables 5–6; Section 8.6
evidence.detail: Results are compiled from other works without a common training-budget, seed or uncertainty specification. No new controlled ablation is presented; evaluation remains multidimensional and protocol-dependent.
